issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must examine the evidence when a trial court has rejected the prosecution case in its entirety and the appellate court reverses the acquittal by accepting substantially the same evidence.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the prosecution evidence as unworthy of belief and acquitted all the accused.
On the State’s appeal against the acquittals, the High Court accepted almost the entire prosecution case and convicted the accused whose acquittals were appealed.
The competing courts’ assessments left little common ground, and the convictions were challenged before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: In these circumstances, the Supreme Court had to examine the evidence to determine whether an error of law or fact vitiated the High Court’s findings.
issues.legal_principle: In appeals arising from convictions entered after reversal of acquittals, the Supreme Court ordinarily does not reappreciate evidence in special-leave appeals, but must examine it where the trial court rejected the whole prosecution case and the appellate court relied on almost the whole of it, so as to determine whether the appellate findings are vitiated by an error of law or fact.

predicates.appeal_from_reversed_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from convictions entered after an appellate court reversed an acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_rejected_entire_case: The trial court rejected the prosecution case in its entirety and acquitted the accused.
predicates.appellate_court_accepted_most_evidence: The appellate court accepted substantially the same prosecution evidence that the trial court had rejected.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows convictions entered after a trial-wide acquittal was reversed on substantially the same evidence, the evidence must be examined for errors that could vitiate the appellate findings.

issues.legal_issue: Partisan evidence in a factional group-violence case cannot be rejected solely because the witnesses are partisan, but must be scrutinised with particular care.
material_facts: The occurrence took place amid a longstanding dispute between rival village factions.
Many prosecution witnesses were related to one another or belonged to the faction opposed to the accused.
The trial court rejected the prosecution evidence as partisan, while the High Court relied on much of it.
issues.conclusion: The partisan character of the evidence did not justify rejecting it wholesale; the evidence required careful scrutiny for discrepancies, genuineness and probability.
issues.legal_principle: Partisan evidence is not to be discarded merely because it is partisan; the court must scrutinise it with more than ordinary care, including whether it contains discrepancies, appears genuine and presents a probable account. The Court relied on R. Kondaiah v. State of A.P. and referred to Masalti v. State of U.P. for a workable approach to evidence in a large group occurrence.

predicates.criminal_case_with_partisan_witnesses: The criminal prosecution relies on witnesses who belong to, or are aligned with, one side of the dispute.
predicates.factional_group_occurrence: The alleged offence occurred in a group confrontation arising from opposing factions.

issues.definition: In a criminal group occurrence involving partisan witnesses, their alignment alone does not justify rejection of their evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Mere presence at an unlawful assembly does not establish membership when a person may have been only a spectator.
material_facts: The incident occurred in a village where an unusual and serious event could draw curious spectators.
A large crowd gathered, and the evidence did not establish that every person present participated in the occurrence or shared the assembly’s purpose.
The Court found that some accused treated as assembly members were in fact mere spectators.
issues.conclusion: Mere presence at the scene or in a crowd was not enough to establish membership in the unlawful assembly.
issues.legal_principle: For the purposes of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, mere presence in an assembly is not by itself proof of membership; the court must distinguish members from people who were merely spectators. The Court relied on Masalti v. State of U.P. in addressing proof of individual roles in a large assembly.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The proceeding concerns alleged membership of an unlawful assembly and liability for offences associated with it.
predicates.person_was_only_present_as_spectator: The person was present at the occurrence only as a spectator and was not shown to have joined the assembly.

issues.definition: In an unlawful-assembly case, presence as a spectator does not establish that the person was a member of the assembly.

issues.legal_issue: Vicarious liability for an offence committed by an unlawful assembly requires established membership and either participation in the offence or knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed in pursuit of the assembly’s common object.
material_facts: The prosecution sought to impose liability for offences committed during a large group occurrence.
The Court distinguished those whose membership was established from people who were merely present.
The Court stated that a member’s overt act need not be proved if the member knew that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object and remained a member.
issues.conclusion: A member of an unlawful assembly is vicariously liable only where membership is established and the member either participates in the offence or has the requisite knowledge that it is likely to be committed in pursuit of the common object.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code attaches vicarious liability to a member of an unlawful assembly who participates by an overt act or knows that the offence is likely to be committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object and becomes or continues to remain a member. Mere presence does not establish membership.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_case and membership_established and (overt_act_participation or (knew_offence_likely_in_common_object and continued_as_member))

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The proceeding concerns vicarious liability for an offence committed by an alleged unlawful assembly.
predicates.membership_established: The person’s membership in the unlawful assembly is clearly established.
predicates.overt_act_participation: The person participated in the commission of the offence by an overt act.
predicates.knew_offence_likely_in_common_object: The person knew that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object.
predicates.continued_as_member: The person became or continued to remain a member of the unlawful assembly.

issues.definition: A person whose membership is established is vicariously liable when that person either participates in the offence or remains a member with knowledge that the offence is likely to occur in pursuit of the common object.

issues.legal_issue: A member of an unlawful assembly is not liable for every separate assault committed during a group occurrence unless the assault was in prosecution of the common object or the member knew it was likely to occur in prosecution of that object.
material_facts: The occurrence involved a large crowd and assaults on different people at different points.
The Court found that the assembly formed to attack and beat the deceased, but that did not establish that all members shared a common object encompassing every separate assault on other people.

Some convictions for specific assaults had been imposed on other members with the aid of Section 149 despite no adequate basis to attribute those assaults to the assembly’s common object or the members’ knowledge.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for the separate assaults could not be sustained against the other accused through vicarious liability merely because they were members of the assembly.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, liability for an offence committed by one member extends to other members only when the offence is committed in prosecution of the common object or the other members knew it was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. A stray or separate assault in a large crowd does not, without that connection, establish such liability.

rule.if: unlawful_assembly_case and separate_individual_assault and not (assault_in_prosecution_of_common_object or members_knew_assault_likely_in_common_object)

predicates.unlawful_assembly_case: The proceeding concerns liability for an offence attributed to members of an unlawful assembly.
predicates.separate_individual_assault: An individual member committed a separate assault during the group occurrence.
predicates.assault_in_prosecution_of_common_object: The assault was committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object.
predicates.members_knew_assault_likely_in_common_ob: The other members knew that the assault was likely to be committed in prosecution of the assembly’s common object.

issues.definition: A separate assault is not imputed to all assembly members when it was outside the common object and the members did not know it was likely to occur in pursuit of that object.

issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction based on an accused’s attributed individual assault cannot stand when the evidence does not satisfactorily establish that person’s role.
material_facts: The High Court convicted several accused of murder with common-intention liability on the basis that each had actively participated in the assault on the deceased.
The evidence concerning the alleged acts varied by accused and included unsupported testimony, material omissions, or conflicts with medical evidence.
The Supreme Court examined the evidence against each accused separately and found the charge proved against some but not others.
issues.conclusion: The murder convictions were sustained only where the evidence satisfactorily established the accused’s participation in the assault; they were set aside where the individual role was not satisfactorily established.
issues.legal_principle: Where a conviction under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code rests on an accused’s active participation by an attributed act, the evidence of that person’s role must be assessed individually and must satisfactorily establish the participation. In examining a large group occurrence, the Court also referred to the workable approach in Masalti v. State of U.P.

predicates.appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal against a murder conviction entered after an acquittal was reversed.
predicates.conviction_based_on_attributed_individua: The conviction rests on a finding that the accused personally participated through an attributed assault.
predicates.individual_role_not_satisfactorily_estab: The evidence, assessed for that accused, does not satisfactorily establish the attributed role.

issues.definition: On an appeal against a murder conviction resting on an attributed personal assault, the conviction is not sustained if the evidence does not satisfactorily establish that accused’s role.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction cannot be maintained where it would produce inconsistent and unequal treatment of similarly situated members after comparable acquittals have become final.
material_facts: The High Court treated some accused as members of the unlawful assembly but did not convict certain similarly situated members of the related group-liability offence.
The acquittals of those members were not challenged by the State and had become final.
The Supreme Court considered that maintaining the remaining convictions would be inconsistent and would treat similarly situated accused unequally.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the remaining similarly situated accused for the group-liability offence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The finality of unchallenged acquittals prevents the court from convicting those acquitted persons in the accused’s appeal; where maintaining convictions against similarly situated members would be self-contradictory and unequal, those convictions must also be set aside. The Court considered liability under Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and the procedural finality of the unchallenged acquittals.

predicates.appeal_against_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by an accused against a conviction.
predicates.comparable_acquittals_became_final: Acquittals of similarly situated persons for the comparable offence were not challenged and became final.
predicates.conviction_would_create_inconsistent_une: Maintaining the appellant’s conviction would produce inconsistent findings or unequal treatment of similarly situated persons.

issues.definition: A conviction is set aside when comparable acquittals have become final and retaining the conviction would treat similarly situated persons inconsistently and unequally.
